newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says no formal Hong Kong invite to Albright.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says no formal Hong Kong invite to Albright.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen raised the possibility of Secretary of State Madeleine Albright witnessing Hong Kong's return to China by Britain but there has been no formal invitation, a State Department official said on Tuesday.
Even if a formal invitation is forthcoming, however, some U.S. officials believe it is unlikely Albright would attend festivities surrounding the turnover, which takes place at midnight on June 30.
The State Department official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Qian raised the issue with Albright when she visited Beijing for the first time as secretary of state on Feb. 24.
"It came up that she had never been to Hong Kong and Qian said perhaps she should visit on July 1," the official said.

As it was clear Britain and China were still working on details of the handover ceremony, "it was not a formal invitation. She has not been formally invited" and hence the United States does not have a formal invitation to which to respond, he added.

Albright has been critical of China's handling of Hong Kong in the runup to the handover, and has warned Beijing the United States will be watching closely to see if China keeps its promises to allow the British colony to preserve a high degree of autonomy and civil freedoms.
Hong Kong radio reported earlier on Tuesday that a Hong Kong politician said Qian had invited Albright to witness the colony's return to China by Britain.
Cheng Yiu-tong, a Hong Kong delegate to China's parliament, quoted Qian as saying he extended the invitation when the two met in Beijing last week, the radio said.

This would make Albright the first foreign dignitary named by either Britain or China as a guest at the historic event, scheduled for midnight on June 30. Officially, London and Beijing have not agreed on a guest list.
Cheng attended a meeting in Beijing where Qian met Hong Kong deputies of the parliament, the National People's Congress.
Qian was quoted as saying he wanted to prove to Albright that accusations leveled against China by some people in Hong Kong were false.

He accused some people in the territory of fabricating charges that Beijing would be flouting the law by dissolving the territory's present legislature and repealing or amending some human rights laws, the radio said.
